<explanation>
Based on your project’s file tree and README, RAGLite is a dedicated Python toolkit for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that allows users to plug in any LLM provider, choose between PostgreSQL or SQLite for storing search information, and even extend retrieval with customizable features (like chat frontends via Chainlit or an MCP server). Here’s a detailed explanation on how to create a system design diagram that accurately reflects its architecture:

1. Identify the Main Components
   • Core RAG Engine: At the heart of the project lies the orchestration of retrieval and generation flows. Modules such as _rag.py, _embed.py, _search.py, _split_chunks.py, and _split_sentences.py make up the core pipeline that performs document ingestion, search (hybrid, keyword, vector), reranking, and generation.
   • Database & Storage: The components in _database.py manage interactions with either PostgreSQL or SQLite. This part is responsible for storing documents, indexes, and evaluations.
   • LLM & Embedding Integrations: With support for multiple LLM providers through integration with LiteLLM and specific modules like _lazy_llama.py and _litellm.py, as well as embedding utilities, these layers manage the communication with external language models and embedding tools.
   • Configuration & CLI: Module _config.py centralizes configurable parameters (database URL, LLM identifiers, embedder details) while _cli.py exposes command-line interface capabilities for both running pipelines and server options.
   • External Interfaces and Extensions: 
         - Chat & Frontend Integration: Modules like _chainlit.py support a chainlit powered ChatGPT-like front end.
         - Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server: Implemented via _mcp.py, this enables connections for MCP clients like Claude desktop.
         - Utility and Conversion Tools: Modules such as _markdown.py (for PDF-to-Markdown conversion) facilitate document preprocessing.
         - Query Adapter: The _query_adapter.py encapsulates the optimized query adapter functionality, solving a closed-form problem to adjust retrieval requests.
   • Testing and Validation: The tests directory contains scripts that validate the functionality of these components.

2. Mapping Relationships and Interactions
   • User interaction (CLI, Chat frontend, or MCP calls) will trigger the configuration loader and then push commands into the RAG pipeline.
   • The RAG pipeline begins with document insertion and conversion (via _extract.py, _split_chunks.py, etc.), where documents are ingested, processed, and stored into the database.
   • For retrieval, components perform different types of search (hybrid, keyword, vector) using _search.py combined with reranking logic (with support from external packages).
   • Once relevant chunks are retrieved, the LLM integration layer (including _litellm.py and _lazy_llama.py) generates responses, possibly after applying any query adaptations computed in _query_adapter.py.
   • Optional modules (chainlit and MCP) demonstrate how the toolkit can serve responses via a frontend or expose tool endpoints for LLMs.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles
   • Modularity and Layering: Each functional responsibility is encapsulated in its own module. This separation supports extensibility (e.g., adding new LLM providers or reranker implementations).
   • Configurable Pipeline: The design allows for both “adaptive” and “programmable” RAG flows, making it flexible for different use cases.
   • Extensibility and Integration: By providing options such as Chainlit integration for ChatGPT-like frontends and an MCP server, the toolkit is built to be easily integrated into larger stacks or to serve as a building block for more complex systems.

4. Key Technologies and Libraries to Note
   • Python’s standard ecosystem for packaging and dependency management with pyproject.toml.
   • Docker, Dev Containers, and GitHub workflows for development, testing, and deployment.
   • External tools like LiteLLM, rerankers, PDF conversion libraries (pdftext, pypdfium2), and the Chainlit frontend.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram to RAGLite
   • For a full-stack RAG application: Emphasize the clear separation between document ingestion, the search/indexing backend (database and embedding layers), and the dynamic response generation using LLMs.
   • For external integrations: Clearly display the optional frontends (ChatGPT-like UI via Chainlit) and the MCP server that extends interaction to other languages.
   • Illustrate the flexibility in choosing database backends, LLM providers, and embedder/reranker tools. Note how configuration (via _config.py) ties these together.

6. Instructions on Crafting the Diagram
   • Use clear, discrete boxes for each major component:
         ◦ “CLI/Config Layer” that reads configuration and kicks off commands.
         ◦ “Document Ingestion & Preprocessing” (covering PDF/Markdown conversion and chunking).
         ◦ “Storage/Database” for document storage and search index management.
         ◦ “Search & Retrieval Logic” for keyword, vector, and hybrid search operations as well as reranking.
         ◦ “LLM Integration & Generation” which coordinates with LLM providers and applies any query adaptation.
         ◦ “Extensions” such as the MCP server and Chat frontend integration.
   • Use directional arrows to depict data flow (e.g., user input → document insertion → retrieval → generation → response).
   • Consider color coding: one color for ingestion/preprocessing components, a different one for search and retrieval mechanisms, and another for output/generation and integration interfaces.
   • Clearly label each component with its purpose and, where applicable, note key modules (e.g., label “Query Adapter (_query_adapter.py)” within the search layer).
   • Optionally include icons or annotations for external libraries such as LiteLLM, rerankers, and specific database technologies (PostgreSQL/SQLite).

7. Emphasis on Detail
   • Include as many components as possible to capture the modular design of RAGLite. Even if some internals are small utility functions, showing their group (like “document splitting”, “embedding”, “evaluation routines”) helps in understanding overall workflow.
   • You need to show both the “adaptive” (LLM deciding retrieval on-the-fly) and “programmable” pipeline options, perhaps using dashed vs. solid arrows to denote optional/alternate flows.
   • Make sure the diagram reflects deployment aspects too – include the containerization elements (Dockerfile, dev container configurations) as a side note, so it’s clear that the system is prepared for scalable development and deployment.

By following these guidelines, you can produce a comprehensive system design diagram that not only maps out the main software modules from the “src” folder but also highlights the user interactions, configurable pipelines, and extensibility aspects (such as optional Chainlit and MCP integrations). This detailed diagram will aid stakeholders in fully understanding RAGLite’s architectural decisions and integration points.
</explanation>
